key_terms.meaning: The path command → linkage → surface deflection → airload → aircraft motion; break any link and the aircraft stops obeying the pilot.
The aerodynamic torque about a control surface's hinge line, in newton-metres (N·m); it is what the pilot or actuator must overcome.
Stick travel per unit surface rotation, in mm per degree or m per radian; with no friction the stick force is F = H ÷ G.
A stiff tube that carries a command in compression as well as tension, so it needs guides and lost-motion-free joints.
Steel cables in matched pairs running over pulleys; each cable carries only tension, so a return path is compulsory.
An adjustable threaded link that sets and holds cable tension so both cables of a pair stay taut.
A pivoted lever that changes the direction of a rod or cable run and can also change the mechanical advantage.
A system that keeps the mechanical link and adds a hydraulic boost, so the pilot feels a reduced share of the hinge moment.
A system where actuators alone move the surface; the mechanical link is gone and artificial feel must be added.
A powered control whose actuator will not back-drive the cockpit, so surface loads are never felt by the pilot directly.
H = q S c C<sub>h</sub>, with q = ½ρV²: grows with V² and with the cube of aircraft size.
Total hinge moment ÷ the pilot’s share in a power-assisted control; 30.6 in the elevator example.
An artificial feel unit that makes stick force proportional to dynamic pressure q = ½ρV², imitating the feel of a mechanical aircraft.
A tab driven by the pilot while the main surface floats; the tab’s air load swings the surface the opposite way, so a small stick force moves a large surface.
A tab geared to move the same way as the surface; it raises the hinge moment, giving a stabilator a positive stick-force gradient and preventing over-control.
A system where pilot inputs become electrical signals to computers that command hydraulic or electric actuators.
The software rule that converts pilot demand and sensor data into surface commands, shaping gain with speed, altitude and configuration.
Several computers and sensor lanes compute together and a majority vote rejects a faulty lane, so one failure does not change the command.
FBW whose signal path is optical fibre instead of wire, giving immunity to electromagnetic interference and no conductive path for lightning.
All k lanes fail: p<sup>k</sup>; triplex majority lost ≈ 3p²; quadruplex majority lost ≈ 4p³.
A closed loop that compares commanded with measured attitude or path and drives the servos itself, without the pilot's hand.
A servo loop that moves the throttle levers to hold a commanded speed, thrust or Mach number.
δ<sub>a</sub> = K<sub>p</sub> e − K<sub>r</sub> p: proportional term on the bank error, rate term for damping.
Use of the flight control system for load alleviation, flutter suppression, ride smoothing and relaxed static stability, not just pilot following.
SM = (x<sub>np</sub> − x<sub>cg</sub>) ÷ c̄; relaxed static stability makes it small or negative.
Full Authority Digital Engine Control: a digital computer with full authority over fuel flow and engine geometry, replacing hydro-mechanical scheduling.
N1<sub>c</sub> = N1 ÷ √θ, θ = T1 ÷ 288.15 K; the FADEC rating holds N1<sub>c</sub>, so physical N1 rises on a hot day.

takeaways: An aircraft does not hold an attitude or path by itself, so a control chain must carry the cockpit demand to a surface: command, linkage or signal, surface, airload, motion.
Gearing links force and moment: with no friction, stick force F = H ÷ G, so the pilot’s 60 N through 0.2750 m/rad holds only 16.5 N·m.
Rods carry push and pull but are sized by buckling; cables carry pull only, so they run in matched pairs with turnbuckles and tension regulators.
Hinge moment H = q S c C<sub>h</sub> grows with V² and with the cube of size, so above a certain size and speed hydraulics supplies the force and the pilot only the command.
An irreversible powered control must be given artificial feel: Q-feel makes stick force rise with dynamic pressure, a bob weight adds feel per g, and tabs do it aerodynamically on manual surfaces.
Fly-by-wire replaces the linkage with sensors, computers and control laws, giving weight saving and envelope protection; it pays with redundant lanes, power and validated software.
Lane counting is a probability argument: a triplex loses its voting majority at about 3p², a quadruplex at about 4p³.

An autopilot closes the same loop with sensors and servos: a fast inner loop holds attitude and rate, a slower outer loop holds heading, altitude or a radio path; the auto-throttle closes the speed loop on thrust.
Active control technology uses the same computers to supply stability (relaxed static stability) and to cut gust and manoeuvre loads, allowing a smaller tail and a lighter wing.
Engine control is its own fast loop: the FADEC holds a corrected fan speed for the selected rating and every limit, so the same lever gives less thrust on a hot day.
bank_note: Long answers here are usually built around one chain (command, linkage or signal, actuator, surface, airload) plus the reasons a given system replaced the previous one, so draw the block diagram and then justify each block. Most syllabi ask for the components and their functions, and for the advantages of each newer system.

bank.q: Explain why an aircraft needs a flight control system at all. Describe the chain from cockpit input to aircraft motion and name the quantity each link must handle.
outline: Aircraft does not hold a wanted attitude or path by itself; disturbances and trim changes act continuously
Chain: pilot command → linkage or signal → surface deflection → aerodynamic force and hinge moment → aircraft motion
Feedback to the pilot through feel, or through sensors in a powered system
Distinguish control (short-term attitude) from trim and from stability
answer: The need. An aircraft left alone does not hold an attitude, a heading or a path. Gusts, thrust changes, fuel burn that moves the centre of gravity, and flap or gear changes all disturb it. The pilot, or later an autopilot, must be able to (i) command a rotation about each axis, (ii) trim a steady out-of-balance moment so it can be held without effort, and (iii) on large aircraft, apply forces no human arm can supply.

answer.text: Axes and surfaces. The flight control system commands the three rotations; translation follows from attitude and thrust.
The chain and the quantity in each link. Draw it as a block diagram from pilot to aircraft, with a dashed return path for feel and sight.

head: Link
What it does
Quantity it handles
rows: turns the hand movement into linkage movement
travel, set by the gearing G (mm per degree)
carries the command to the tail or wing
deflection δ (degrees) against hinge moment H (N·m)
rotates about its centre of gravity
moment about the CG (N·m), then angular rate (deg/s)
pilot feels and sees the result

answer: How the links connect. With no friction, the work at the stick equals the work at the surface, F × stick travel = H × surface rotation, so F = H ÷ G. Example: 120 mm of column for 25° of elevator gives G = 4.8 mm/deg = 0.2750 m/rad; a 60 N pull holds H = 60 × 0.2750 = 16.50 N·m; with an 80 mm horn the rod carries 16.50 ÷ 0.080 = 206.3 N.

Feedback. In a manual system the hinge moment comes back up the linkage, so the pilot feels the airload. In a powered system the actuator absorbs it and feel must be made artificially. In fly-by-wire, sensors (gyros, accelerometers, air data) close the loop inside the computer.

Control, trim and stability are different jobs. Control is the short-term change of attitude. Trim holds a steady deflection with no stick force (a trim tab or an adjustable stabilizer). Stability is the aircraft’s own tendency to return after a disturbance; the control system works with it, and in relaxed-stability aircraft supplies part of it.

Closing check. The example’s numbers balance: 60 N × 120 mm = 7200 N·mm at the stick, and 206.3 N × 34.9 mm (80 mm × 0.4363 rad) = 7200 N·mm at the horn, so no work is created or lost in the ideal linkage.

bank.q: List the main components of a conventional flight control system and state the function of each.
outline: Cockpit controls: stick or wheel, pedals, throttle
Linkage: rods, cables, pulleys, bell cranks, quadrants, turnbuckles
Surface attachments: horns, hinges, control surface itself
Feel and trim devices: trim tabs, bungees, downsprings
Stops, locks and gust locks; position indicators
answer: Frame the answer. A conventional (mechanical) system is a chain of parts from the cockpit to each surface, as on a Cessna 172R: control wheel on a column, rudder pedals, throttle and mixture, and a manual trim wheel. Group the parts by job and give one function each.

head: Part
Function
rows: Control column with wheel or stick
pitch input fore and aft, roll input by turning or moving sideways
yaw input; on the ground they also steer the nosewheel
sets the trim tab so a steady deflection needs no force

head: Part
Function
rows: tube carrying push and pull; sized against buckling
stranded steel carrying pull only, so used in matched pairs
guides a cable round a corner; changes direction, not tension
keep a cable in line through structure; let it pass a pressure bulkhead
pivoted lever that turns the direction of a run and can change the motion ratio
sector lever that turns cable travel into rotation, or back
threaded barrel that sets cable tension during rigging
spring device that keeps cable tension nearly constant as temperature changes

head: Part
Function
rows: lever arm where the rod or cable attaches; sets the moment arm about the hinge
pivot about which the surface rotates
aileron, elevator or rudder that deflects into the airflow

answer: Protection and adjustment. Control stops limit surface travel so the structure is not over-stressed; a gust lock holds the surfaces on the ground so wind cannot slam them against the stops; rigging pins hold controls and surfaces at neutral while tensions are set.
Feel and trim devices. Trim tabs hold a steady deflection; on some light aircraft a bungee or downspring in the elevator circuit shapes the stick force.

Typical chain to quote. Pull the column back; a short rod turns a bell crank under the floor; two cables run aft over pulleys, each with a turnbuckle; the cable pulls the elevator horn and the elevator rises. Pushing reverses it, with the other cable pulling.

Closing check. Every part named has one function and sits in one of the five groups; the answer covers the cockpit end, the transmission, the surface end, protection and trim, which is what a 10-mark list question expects.

bank.q: Compare the push-pull rod system with the cable-pulley system for primary flight controls: construction, load paths, friction, weight and maintenance.
outline: Rod: tube in tension and compression, needs guides and bell cranks, high stiffness, low stretch, heavier over long runs
Cable: tension only, always in matched pairs, pulleys, turnbuckles, fairleads, tension regulators
Friction and backlash: pulleys and fairleads add friction; rods add many joints
Routing, thermal expansion, pre-tension, inspection for fraying or rod-end wear
Which suits a small trainer and which suits a large transport
answer: Construction of a rod run. A thin metal tube with a ball-jointed rod end at each end. The ball lets the rod tilt, so it carries only axial push or pull and no bending. Bell cranks turn corners and can change the motion ratio; idler levers and guides support long runs.

Construction of a cable run. Stranded steel cable in a closed loop of two cables, one pulling each way. Pulleys turn corners, fairleads keep the cable in line, pressure seals pass it through a bulkhead, turnbuckles set pre-tension and a tension regulator holds it nearly constant as the airframe expands.

Load paths. A rod carries tension and compression, so one rod drives the surface both ways. In compression a long tube buckles before its material fails. A cable carries tension only, so the return movement needs the second cable, kept under pre-tension so there is no lost motion when the demand reverses.

answer.text: Numbers (same 3 m run, 1.5 kN). Cable, 6 mm², E = 200 GPa: ΔL = FL ÷ (AE) = 1500 × 3 ÷ (6 × 10⁻⁶ × 200 × 10⁹) = 3.75 mm of stretch. Rod, aluminium tube 20/18 mm, E = 70 GPa: A = 59.7 mm², σ = 25.1 MPa, but I = 2701 mm⁴ gives an Euler load of only 207 N over 3 m. With guides, Pcr grows with the square of the number of bays:

answer: Friction and backlash. Every pulley and fairlead adds friction, so a long cable run feels heavy and sticky; cable stretch and pulley clearance give lost motion. A rod run has little friction but backlash at every rod end and bell-crank bearing. Backlash that grows can lower the flutter speed of a surface.

Weight and routing. Cables are light over long runs and follow curved paths around structure. Rods need straight lines, many bell cranks and strong supports, so they are heavy over long runs but stiff and precise over short ones.

Temperature. An aluminium airframe expands more than steel cable, so cable tension changes with temperature; the tension regulator corrects it. Rods change length too, which rigging adjustment allows for.

head: Push-pull rod
Cable-pulley
rows: tension, broken wires, pulley freedom, fairlead wear
jam if structure bends into the path; buckling
cable jumps a pulley or wears through at a fairlead
set length at adjustable rod ends
set tension at turnbuckles with rigging pins in

answer: Which suits which. A small trainer uses both: rods for short runs near the cockpit and ailerons, cables for the long run to the tail. On a large transport the long runs favour cables, but the forces outgrow the pilot, so the cables or rods only carry the command to hydraulic actuators; fly-by-wire types replace them with wires.

Closing check. The comparison is complete on all five headings asked (construction, load path, friction, weight, maintenance), and the numbers show the deciding limits: about 3.75 mm of stretch for the cable, and buckling, not the 25.1 MPa stress, for the rod.

bank.q: Explain the Q-feel system. Why is it needed, how does it work, and how does it produce stick force proportional to dynamic pressure?
outline: Irreversible powered control gives no hinge moment feedback to the pilot
q = ½ρV²: the aircraft responds more sharply at higher q, so feel must rise too
Q-feel unit uses impact pressure to load a spring cartridge in the stick circuit
Result: stick force per unit deflection rises with q; bob weight adds feel per g
Compare with aerodynamic feel from a tab
answer: Why feel is lost. In a fully powered (irreversible) control, the closed servo valve traps fluid and the actuator carries the whole hinge moment. Air loads never reach the stick, so the pilot has no sense of airspeed or of how hard the surface is working.

Why a plain spring is not enough. The aircraft’s response to one degree of surface grows with dynamic pressure q = ½ρV². A fixed spring gives the same force at every speed, so at high q a light pull commands a large manoeuvre and can over-stress the airframe, while at low q the aircraft feels sluggish.

head: Element
Job
rows: their difference is impact pressure, which gives q
converts q into a feel demand, for example 3 N per kPa
moves the anchor of a spring cartridge, stiffening it as q rises
Spring cartridge in the stick circuit
stick force F = k(q) × x for a stick displacement x
adds force in proportion to load factor n, so the pilot feels each g
moves the zero-force point, so the trimmed position needs no force

answer: How force follows q. Because the spring rate k is made proportional to q, the force for a given stick displacement rises with V², just as a natural hinge moment would on a manual aircraft. The unit loads only the stick; the surface still moves to the commanded angle.

answer.text: Worked numbers. Gradient 3 N per kPa above trim, trimmed (zero force) at 75 m/s, ρ = 1.225 kg/m³:

answer: Why the bob weight is still needed. In a pull-up at constant speed, q does not change, so the Q-feel force would stay the same at 1 g and at 3 g. The bob weight adds force with load factor and tells the pilot how hard the aircraft is being pulled.
Failure case. If the feel unit loses its pressure input, the stick becomes light at high speed, the dangerous direction; such units have a failure warning and the crew limits speed.

Aerodynamic feel from tabs. On manual or boosted surfaces the same goal is reached without a feel unit: an anti-servo tab, geared to move with the surface, raises the hinge moment and gives stick force that rises naturally with q. In fly-by-wire aircraft the gradient is written in software and a motor loads the stick.

Closing check. q rose 4 times from 75 to 150 m/s (13.781 ÷ 3.445 = 4.00), but the force is counted from trim, so it rose from 0 to 31.0 N; from 150 to 250 m/s the extra 24.5 kPa adds 3 × 24.5 = 73.5 N, giving 104.5 N.

bank.q: What is a servo tab? Explain how a small tab force moves a large surface, and how the anti-servo tab differs.
outline: Tab hinged at the trailing edge of the main surface
Pilot moves the tab; tab air load creates a moment about the main surface hinge
Main surface follows, so pilot force depends on tab size and gearing, not on surface area
Anti-servo tab moves the same way as the surface, adding feel and damping on stabilators
Trim tab is set to a fixed deflection to relieve steady stick force
answer: Definition. A servo tab is a small hinged aerofoil at the trailing edge of a primary surface. In a servo tab system the pilot’s linkage drives only the tab; the main surface floats freely on its hinge.

How the small force moves the large surface. The pilot moves the tab trailing edge up. The airflow pushes the tab down; that force acts at the trailing edge, on a long arm behind the main hinge, and swings the main surface trailing edge down, the opposite way to the tab. The surface settles where its own hinge moment balances the tab’s moment.

Why the force is small. The pilot only has to hold the tab’s own hinge moment, which is small because the tab chord is short. So stick force depends on tab size and gearing, not on the size of the main surface; that is how large manual aircraft were flown by tab.

answer.text: Moment balance, with assumed numbers. Suppose the tab’s air load is 200 N, acting 0.60 m behind the main hinge and 0.02 m behind the tab’s own hinge:
answer.pre:
moment the tab puts on the main surface   200 × 0.60 = 120 N·m
moment the pilot must hold on the tab      200 × 0.02 =   4 N·m
reduction in what the pilot holds          120 ÷ 4    =  30 times

head: Tab
Moves
Job
rows: driven by the pilot; surface goes the opposite way
opposite to the surface, linked to fixed structure
cuts hinge moment, assists the pilot
opposite to the surface once the spring load is exceeded
set by the pilot and left there
holds a steady deflection with no force

answer: Anti-servo tab. It is geared to move in the same direction as the surface, so it increases the hinge moment and resists the pilot. A stabilator (all-moving tail, as on the Piper PA-28) pivots near its own aerodynamic centre, so its hinge moment is small; without the tab the stick would be too light and the tail could be over-controlled. The tab gives a positive stick-force gradient and damps the surface against gusts.

Closing check. Servo and geared tabs move opposite to the surface and assist; the anti-servo tab moves with the surface and resists. Memory line: a servo tab saves muscle, an anti-servo tab gives back information.

bank.q: Describe a digital fly-by-wire system. Explain the signal path and the role of control laws and redundancy.
outline: Pilot input transducers, air data and inertial sensors feed the flight control computers
Computers run control laws; output drives electro-hydraulic or electro-hydrostatic actuators
Control law gives rate command, C*, gain scheduling with q̄ and configuration, envelope protection
Redundancy: multiple lanes, dissimilar hardware and software, majority voting, reversion modes
Advantages: weight, no rigging or friction, envelope protection; disadvantages: software certification, power dependence
answer: Definition. Digital fly-by-wire (DFBW) replaces the mechanical linkage between cockpit and surfaces with sensors, digital flight control computers (FCCs) and wires. The pilot’s input becomes a demand; the computers decide how far each surface moves.

answer.text: Signal path. Draw it as a block diagram with a feedback path from the aircraft back to the sensors.

head: Block
What passes through it
rows: Sidestick or column with position transducers
pilot demand, for example a pitch rate in deg/s
p, q, r (deg/s), n<sub>z</sub> (g), V, q̄, α
each computes the same surface command; a voter compares them
surface position command, with its own position loop
motion, measured again by the sensors

answer: Control laws. A control law is the rule that turns demand and sensor data into actuator commands. A rate-command law drives the surface until measured rate equals demanded rate. The C* pitch law blends pitch rate and normal acceleration: pitch rate dominates at low speed, g at high speed, so handling feels the same across the envelope. Gains are scheduled with q̄, Mach and flap setting.

Modes. Normal mode has full envelope protection (stall, overspeed, bank and load-factor limits). Alternate mode loses some protections after failures. Direct mode passes the stick almost straight to the surfaces with no protection.

answer.text: Redundancy, with numbers. Each lane fails with p = 1 × 10⁻⁴ per hour, independently; the target for a catastrophic failure is 1 × 10⁻⁹ per hour.

head: Architecture
Event
Probability per hour
rows: voting majority lost, two or more fail (≈ 3p²)
majority lost, three or more fail (≈ 4p³)

answer: Reading the table. Two good lanes outvote one bad one; after a first failure a triplex has only two lanes, which can detect a disagreement but not tell which is wrong. A quadruplex can still outvote a second failure, so it meets the target with margin. Dissimilar hardware and software, separate power supplies and physically separated wiring guard against one fault taking every lane at once, which the independence assumption ignores.
Why digital. Software can self-check and run built-in test, schedule gains, add protections and be changed without rewiring; analog lanes drifted and could not do this.

head: Advantages
Costs
rows: no cables, pulleys or rigging: weight saved
depends on electrical power and computers
software must be validated to a high assurance level
relaxed static stability allows a smaller tail

answer: Closing check. 3 × (10⁻⁴)² = 3 × 10⁻⁸ and 4 × (10⁻⁴)³ = 4 × 10⁻¹²; only the second is below 10⁻⁹, which is why the lane count and the voting scheme are part of the design, not an afterthought.

bank.q: Explain the operation of an autopilot and of an auto-throttle, and state the advantages of each.
outline: Autopilot: sensor measures attitude or path, comparator forms error against command, computer shapes correction, servo moves surface
Inner loops (pitch rate, roll rate, yaw damping) and outer loops (altitude, heading, radio path)
Modes: wing level, heading select, altitude hold, localizer and glide slope, autoland
Auto-throttle: servo drives thrust levers to hold speed or Mach; TOGA
Advantages: reduced workload, precise tracking, consistent approach speed, fuel saving
answer: The autopilot as a closed loop. The pilot selects a mode and a target. Sensors measure the actual state; the computer subtracts actual from commanded to form an error, shapes a correction and sends it to a servo; the servo moves the surface; the aircraft responds and the sensors see the new state.

Components. Sensors: attitude and rate gyros or an IMU, air data (speed, altitude), radio receivers (VOR, localizer, glide slope), a radio altimeter on approach. Computer: the flight control computer. Servos: electro-hydraulic or electro-mechanical. Mode panel, and a disconnect button that removes servo power.

answer.text: Inner loop law, with numbers. Roll channel δa = Kp e − Kr p, with Kp = 3 deg/deg and Kr = 0.8 s. The aircraft is 4° left of the commanded bank (e = +4°) and already rolling right at p = +2°/s:
answer.pre:
proportional term  3 × 4      = 12.0°
rate term          0.8 × 2    =  1.6°
aileron command    12.0 − 1.6 = 10.4° right

answer: Why the rate term. Proportional control alone would still command 12° as the aircraft approaches the target and overshoot. The rate term removes 1.6° (13 %) because the aircraft is already moving the right way, so it stops smoothly.

Outer loop, with numbers. Heading select from 070° to 110°: bank command 1.0 × 40° = 40°, limited to 25°. Turn rate ω = g tan φ ÷ V = 9.81 × 0.4663 ÷ 120 = 0.0381 rad/s = 2.18°/s. The bank stays at the limit for the first 15° of turn, 15 ÷ 2.18 = 6.9 s, then shrinks with the error. The outer loop hands the inner loop a bank target; the inner loop flies it.

Modes. Pitch and roll hold, altitude hold, heading select, VOR/localizer and glide-slope coupling, and autoland for Category II and III approaches, which needs redundant sensors, computers and servos. A yaw damper sits in the inner loop.

Auto-throttle. It moves the thrust levers only. In speed or Mach hold it compares actual with selected speed and drives the levers to cut the error; rate of change of speed damps the response. TOGA drives the levers to take-off or go-around thrust. The engine control then turns lever position into fuel within all limits. On approach the autopilot holds the glide path with pitch while the auto-throttle holds speed with thrust.

head: Autopilot
Auto-throttle
rows: pilot no longer adjusts thrust through every gust
precise tracking of heading, altitude and radio paths
precise approach speed, so landing distance is predictable
fuel saving by holding the planned speed or Mach

answer: Closing check. δ = 12.0 − 1.6 = 10.4° and 15° ÷ 2.18°/s = 6.9 s; both loops act on errors, the inner one in a fraction of a second, the outer one over several seconds.

bank.q: Explain full authority digital engine control (FADEC). How does it replace a hydro-mechanical fuel control unit?
outline: Engine loop: thrust lever angle in; fuel flow and geometry (VSV, bleed valves) out
Sensors: N1, N2, EGT, fuel flow, inlet pressure and temperature, lever angle
Hydro-mechanical unit uses cams, bellows and a governor to schedule fuel
FADEC: two channels, corrected-speed rating schedules, limits, start sequencing, built-in test
Advantages: precise limits, fuel efficiency, condition monitoring; needs redundant channels and power
answer: What engine control must do. Meet the thrust demand while keeping spool speeds, exhaust gas temperature (EGT) and surge margin inside limits. It acts on fuel flow (fuel metering valve), air flow (variable stator vanes and bleed valves) and, on some engines, the exhaust (nozzle area, thrust reverser).

The hydro-mechanical fuel control unit (FCU). Cams, bellows, levers and a flyweight governor. The lever sets the governed speed; the governor meters fuel to hold it. An acceleration schedule caps fuel during a quick lever movement so the compressor does not surge or the turbine over-heat; a deceleration schedule keeps a minimum flow so the flame stays alight; limiters cut fuel before EGT or speed limits. It is reliable but cannot be retuned easily and has no self-test.

answer.text: The FADEC. A digital engine control with full authority over fuel and geometry, two channels (one active, one standby), its own power supply and built-in test, and no full-authority mechanical backup.

head: Inputs
Outputs
rows: engine data to cockpit and auto-throttle

answer: Ratings and corrected speed. The lever asks for a rating (take-off, maximum continuous, climb, cruise). For each rating the FADEC holds a corrected fan speed N1c = N1 ÷ √θ, with θ = T1 ÷ 288.15 K, trimming fuel to hold it.

answer.text: Worked numbers. Take-off rating N1c = 97.0 %, physical N1 limit 100.0 %:

answer: Reading the numbers. At 40 °C the FADEC holds the 100.0 % limit, so the corrected speed reached is 100.0 ÷ 1.0425 = 95.9 % and take-off thrust is lower. The FCU could not do this calculation; the FADEC does it every few milliseconds and also applies the EGT limit.

How it replaces the FCU. The cams and governor become software schedules; the hydro-mechanical unit shrinks to a fuel metering unit that the FADEC drives. Start sequencing, limit protection and engine data reporting move into the same computer.

head: Hydro-mechanical FCU
FADEC
rows: computed N1, N2 and EGT limits

answer: Closing check. 97.0 × √(313.15 ÷ 288.15) = 97.0 × 1.0425 = 101.1 %, above 100.0 %, so the limit acts; on the cold day 97.0 × 0.9556 = 92.7 %, well inside it.

bank.q: A transport aircraft’s elevator has area 2.4 m², chord 0.5 m and hinge moment coefficient 0.08 at the deflection needed. Find the hinge moment at 75, 150 and 250 m/s at sea level (ρ = 1.225 kg/m³). The linkage gearing is 0.30 m/rad and the pilot can give 300 N for a short time. Decide whether a pilot could move it without hydraulic power, and find the boost ratio needed at 250 m/s.
outline: q = ½ρV² at each speed
Hinge moment H = q S c C<sub>h</sub>
Unboosted stick force F = H ÷ G
Compare with the pilot’s 300 N; pilot share 300 × 0.30 = 90 N·m
Conclude: powered control needed; boost ratio at 250 m/s
answer: Data. S = 2.4 m², c = 0.5 m, Ch = 0.08, ρ = 1.225 kg/m³, G = 0.30 m/rad, pilot force 300 N. Formulas: q = ½ρV², H = q S c Ch, unboosted stick force F = H ÷ G.
Constant part. S c Ch = 2.4 × 0.5 × 0.08 = 0.096 m³, so H = 0.096 q.

Pilot’s capacity. The pilot can hold 300 N × 0.30 m/rad = 90 N·m. Even at 75 m/s the surface needs 330.8 N·m, 3.7 times that; at 250 m/s it needs 3675 N·m, and the unboosted pull would be 12 250 N, about forty times what a person can give.

Could the gearing be raised instead? To hold 3675 N·m with 300 N, G would have to be 3675 ÷ 300 = 12.25 m/rad: about 2 m of stick travel for 10° of elevator, which no cockpit can give. So gearing alone cannot solve it.
Boost ratio at 250 m/s. Boost ratio = total hinge moment ÷ pilot share = 3675 ÷ 90 = 40.8; the hydraulics would supply 3675 − 90 = 3585 N·m, 97.6 % of the load.

Actuator size at 250 m/s. If the actuator works on a 0.10 m arm at 3000 psi (20.7 MPa), its force is 3585 ÷ 0.10 = 35 850 N and its piston area 35 850 ÷ (20.7 × 10⁶) = 1.73 × 10⁻³ m² = 17.3 cm², a bore of about 47 mm, before any margin for valve pressure drop.

Decision. A pilot cannot move this elevator without hydraulic power at any of the three speeds. A power-assisted system with a boost ratio of about 41 would do at 250 m/s, but at that ratio manual reversion would leave the pilot 41 times the normal force. A transport of this size is therefore normally fully powered, with two or three actuators on separate hydraulic systems and artificial feel.
Assumptions. Sea-level density at all speeds; Ch fixed at 0.08 for the deflection needed; no friction; hinge moment at the deflection actually used.
Closing check. H grows with V²: (250 ÷ 75)² = 11.1, and 3675 ÷ 330.8 = 11.1, so the table is consistent.

bank.q: Design the redundancy scheme for a digital fly-by-wire flight control computer of a civil transport and justify the voting scheme you choose. Take one lane’s failure probability as 1 × 10⁻⁴ per flight hour and the target for loss of control as 1 × 10⁻⁹ per flight hour.
outline: Compute simplex, duplex, triplex and quadruplex probabilities
Comparison, threshold and majority vote (2-out-of-3 or 3-out-of-4)
Fail-operational then fail-safe behaviour
Dissimilar hardware and software against common-mode faults
Power, sensor and actuator redundancy, built-in test
Reversion modes and the certification argument
answer: Requirement. Loss of control must be less likely than 1 × 10⁻⁹ per flight hour. One lane fails with p = 1 × 10⁻⁴ per hour, so a single computer is 100 000 times too unreliable. Lanes are assumed to fail independently.

head: Lanes
What the system can still do after failures
Key probability per hour
Meets 10⁻⁹?
rows: detects a disagreement but cannot tell which lane is wrong, so disconnects (fail-safe)
both fail p² = 1 × 10⁻⁸; a disconnect about 2p = 2 × 10⁻⁴
outvotes the first failure (2 of 3); after a second it is duplex
no, if loss of majority means loss of control
outvotes two successive failures (3 of 4, then 2 of 3)

answer: Choice. A quadruplex of command lanes, with majority voting: 3-out-of-4, dropping to 2-out-of-3 after the first failure. It is fail-operational after one failure and still fail-operational (by majority) after a second, then fail-safe. An equal alternative is a triplex plus a dissimilar backup computer and a direct mode, so that the 3 × 10⁻⁸ event leads to a degraded but flyable aircraft, not loss of control.

Voting and monitoring. Each lane computes the surface command; a voter compares the outputs and takes the middle value. A lane that differs from the others by more than a threshold for longer than a set time is declared failed and isolated, so a brief transient does not trip it. Each lane is also split into command and monitor halves that cross-check each other.

Common-mode faults. The independence assumption fails for a software error copied into every lane, a power failure, or a lightning strike on one wiring bundle. Answer: dissimilar processors and separately written software in at least two lane types; lanes on separate electrical buses with battery back-up; wiring routed apart; shielding and lightning protection.

Sensors and actuators. Rate gyros, accelerometers and air data come in three or four sets, with their own voting. Each surface gets two or three actuators on separate hydraulic systems, so a single hydraulic loss does not lose the surface.
Reversion modes. Normal mode with full protection; alternate mode after some failures; direct mode with the stick going almost straight to the surfaces. Each change is announced to the crew.

Built-in test and maintenance. Power-up and continuous built-in test find dormant faults before flight. The probability argument assumes every lane is working at take-off, so the minimum equipment rules forbid dispatch with a failed lane, or only for a limited time.

Certification argument. Show by fault-tree analysis that every path to loss of control is below 10⁻⁹ per hour, including common-mode paths, and show by test that the voting isolates each single failure without a dangerous transient.
Closing check. 4 × (10⁻⁴)³ = 4 × 10⁻¹² is 250 times below 10⁻⁹, while 3 × (10⁻⁴)² = 3 × 10⁻⁸ is 30 times above it; the quadruplex is the smallest lane count that meets the target on its own.

bank.q: A light aircraft elevator moves 30° for 150 mm of column travel. The elevator has S = 1.2 m², c = 0.3 m and C<sub>h</sub> = 0.10 at full deflection at 50 m/s (ρ = 1.225 kg/m³). Its horn arm is 75 mm, and the loaded cable is 4 m long with a metal area of 6 mm² and E = 200 GPa. Find the hinge moment, the stick force, the cable force, the cable stretch and the elevator angle lost to that stretch. Comment on the design.
outline: q and hinge moment H = q S c C<sub>h</sub>
Gearing in m/rad and stick force F = H ÷ G
Cable force = H ÷ horn arm
Stretch ΔL = FL ÷ (AE) and lost angle ΔL ÷ arm
Judge the force and the lost motion; suggest remedies
answer: Dynamic pressure. q = ½ × 1.225 × 50² = 1531.25 Pa.
Gearing. 30° = 0.5236 rad, so G = 0.150 m ÷ 0.5236 rad = 0.2865 m/rad (5 mm per degree).
Stick force. With no friction, F = H ÷ G = 55.13 ÷ 0.2865 = 192.4 N.
Cable force. Assuming the cable pulls at right angles to the horn, force = H ÷ arm = 55.13 ÷ 0.075 = 735 N.
Lost elevator angle. The horn tip falls 2.45 mm short, so the elevator is short by 2.45 ÷ 75 = 0.0327 rad = 1.87°, about 6 % of the 30° commanded.

Comment. 192 N is a heavy pull for a light trainer at full deflection, so the design needs less hinge moment: aerodynamic balance (a horn balance or a set-back hinge) or a geared balance tab would cut Ch; a larger gearing would cut the force but make the response sluggish and the column travel long. The 1.87° lost to stretch is acceptable only if it is repeatable; correct cable pre-tension and a stiffer (larger) cable reduce it.

answer.text: Effect of the remedies, in numbers. A geared balance tab that cuts Ch from 0.10 to 0.06 cuts every force in proportion:

answer: Why the slack cable matters. The other cable of the pair carries only its pre-tension. If that pre-tension is too low, the slack cable can sag and add lost motion when the pilot reverses the demand, on top of the 2.45 mm stretch of the loaded cable.
Closing check. Work at the stick 192.4 N × 0.150 m = 28.86 J equals work at the hinge 55.13 N·m × 0.5236 rad = 28.86 J.

bank.q: Compare mechanical, power-assisted, fully powered and fly-by-wire flight control systems on weight, feel, redundancy, maintenance and envelope protection. Which suits a 2-seat trainer and which suits a large transport?
outline: Force limit of a mechanical system: F = H ÷ G, H grows with V² and size³
Feel: natural, partly natural, artificial by Q-feel, artificial by control law
Redundancy: none, manual reversion, multiple actuators and hydraulics, multi-lane computers
Maintenance: rigging and backlash versus hydraulics versus software and LRUs
Envelope protection only in FBW
Recommendation: trainer mechanical; transport FBW with powered actuators
answer: What drives the choice. Hinge moment H = q S c Ch grows with V² and with the cube of aircraft size, while the pilot can hold only F × G, for example 200 N × 0.30 m/rad = 60 N·m. So the system is chosen by how far the hinge moment outgrows the pilot.

Mechanical. Rods and cables only; the pilot supplies all the force and feels the air load directly. Simple, cheap and fully understood; heavy and frictional on long runs; no redundancy beyond duplicated cables; maintenance is rigging, tension and wear checks.

Power-assisted. The linkage stays and a hydraulic actuator acts in parallel. In the elevator example the hinge moment of 1837.5 N·m against the pilot’s 60 N·m needs a boost ratio of 30.6. The pilot keeps some natural feel; if hydraulics fail, manual reversion is possible at much higher forces and a restricted speed.

Fully powered. Actuators alone move the surface; the control is irreversible, so gusts do not reach the stick but neither does feel, and Q-feel must be added. Two or three actuators per surface on separate hydraulic systems provide the redundancy; jams and rate limits must be designed out.

Fly-by-wire. The linkage is replaced by sensors, computers and wires; actuators are still hydraulic or electro-hydrostatic. Feel comes from sidestick springs and the control law. Redundancy is by three or four lanes with voting; a quadruplex keeps its voting majority to about 4 × 10⁻¹² per hour. It alone gives envelope protection and allows relaxed static stability.

head: Mechanical
Power-assisted
Fully powered
Fly-by-wire
rows: low on small aircraft, high on large
lowest linkage weight; computers and wiring
stall, overspeed, g and bank limits

answer: Analysis of the trend. Each step solves the previous system’s limit and creates a new burden: boost solves force but adds hydraulics; full power solves reversion forces at speed but kills feel; FBW solves weight and rigging and adds protection but makes the aircraft depend on computers, power and validated software.

Recommendation for a 2-seat trainer. Mechanical controls: hinge moments of a few tens of N·m (16.5 N·m in the light-aircraft example) are within a pilot’s strength, natural feel teaches handling, and the system is cheap and easy to inspect; the Cessna 172R is flown this way.

Recommendation for a large transport. Fly-by-wire with fully powered actuators on separate hydraulic and electrical systems, quadruplex or triplex-plus-backup computers, and artificial feel. Hinge moments of thousands of N·m (7350 N·m at 200 m/s in the elevator example) rule out manual control, and the weight saving and protection repay the cost.
Closing check. The deciding numbers are consistent: 60 N·m of pilot capacity covers 16.5 N·m but not 1837.5 N·m, let alone 7350 N·m.

bank.q: Discuss active control technology. How do relaxed static stability, gust and manoeuvre load alleviation and flutter suppression change the aircraft design, and what risks does each introduce?
outline: Relaxed static stability: small or negative static margin, smaller tail, less trim drag, computer supplies stability
Gust and manoeuvre load alleviation reduce wing bending, allowing a lighter wing
Flutter suppression adds damping and extends the speed envelope
Ride smoothing and envelope limiting
Risks: dependence on the control system, failure cases, actuator rate limits, certification
answer: Definition. Active control technology (ACT) uses the flight control computers and surfaces to supply stability and to shape loads, not only to follow the pilot. An aircraft designed around it is a control configured vehicle.

Relaxed static stability (RSS). Static margin SM = (xnp − xcg) ÷ c̄. A conventional aircraft has a positive margin, so the tail pushes down in steady flight and the wing must carry that download as extra lift. RSS moves the CG aft to a small or negative margin; the download falls, trim drag falls and the tail can be smaller. In a fighter the negative margin also makes the aircraft pitch into a turn more readily. Risk: the bare airframe diverges in pitch, so loss of the computers must be extremely improbable (multi-lane FBW).

Gust load alleviation (GLA). Accelerometers sense the gust; a band-pass filter keeps only the gust band (rejecting the steady 1 g and sensor noise); ailerons and spoilers move to unload the wing as the gust arrives.

answer.text: GLA in numbers. Gust limit load 2.5 g cut to 2.0 g, factor of safety 1.5, root bending 2.0 MN·m at 1 g:

answer: Design effect. If this gust case sizes the root, the bending material there can be up to about 20 % lighter, a saving carried for the aircraft’s whole life. Manoeuvre load alleviation does the same for the pilot’s pull by shifting lift inboard as the pull begins.

Flutter suppression. Sensors detect the bending-torsion flutter mode, and a surface is driven so its force is in phase with the mode’s velocity, which adds damping. The design effect is a higher flutter speed for the same structure, or less stiffening mass.
Ride smoothing and envelope limiting. Ride control cuts the response passengers feel in turbulence; envelope limiting keeps α, load factor and q̄ inside limits, giving carefree handling.

head: Function
Main risk
Answer in the design
rows: a wrong or late deflection adds load
show no load is made worse anywhere in the envelope
actuator rate limit adds phase and can drive the mode
actuators fast enough; failure must leave a safe speed limit
structure sized on an active function
airframe must survive with the function switched off

answer: Evaluation. The gains are large and permanent (smaller tail, lighter wing, less fuel), and they come from software on hardware the FBW aircraft already carries. The cost is moved into certification: every function must be shown not to worsen any load and to fail safely. For a FBW transport this is a good trade; for a mechanical aircraft ACT is not possible at all.
Closing check. 1.5 × 2.5 = 3.75 g and 1.5 × 2.0 = 3.0 g; 2.0 × 3.75 = 7.5 MN·m and 2.0 × 3.0 = 6.0 MN·m; both cuts are 20 %, as they must be when bending is proportional to load factor.

bank.q: Evaluate fly-by-light against fly-by-wire. State the physical reasons for its advantages and the practical reasons it is not universal.
outline: FBW signal path is electrical wire; FBL uses optical fibre
Advantages: immune to EMI and lightning-induced currents, no ground loops, no spark, light, high bandwidth
Problems: connectors and splices, bend radius, optical power budget, actuators still need power
Optical-to-electrical interfaces add parts
Where FBL suits; one production example
answer: What changes. Fly-by-light (FBL) keeps the FBW architecture (sensors, computers, control laws, powered actuators) and replaces only the signal wires with optical fibre. The actuators still need hydraulic or electrical power.

Why the advantages are physical. A fibre carries light in glass, not current in a conductor. So a changing magnetic field (EMI, high-intensity radiated fields, lightning) induces no current in it; there are no ground loops; a damaged fibre cannot spark near fuel; and light pulses carry far higher data rates than a copper pair.
Weight. A FBW aircraft needs heavy shielding and lightning protection on its signal wiring; fibre needs none for its signal, so the harness is lighter.

answer.text: Why it is not universal: the optical power budget. Example with assumed values: transmitter −10 dBm, receiver sensitivity −30 dBm (20 dB available); 6 connectors at 0.75 dB; 200 m of fibre at 3 dB/km; 3 dB margin for ageing.
answer.pre:
connectors  6 × 0.75   = 4.5 dB
fibre       0.2 × 3    = 0.6 dB
margin                 = 3.0 dB
total                  = 8.1 dB  ≤ 20 dB available: link closes

answer: Reading the budget. Most loss is at connectors, not in the fibre, so every extra break in the run for maintenance costs budget; a dirty or damaged connector can lose several dB and close the link.

Other practical problems. Fibre has a minimum bend radius, which limits routing through tight structure; repair needs special splicing tools and training; every computer and actuator needs an optical-to-electrical interface, which adds parts and failure points; and decades of certified copper-wire FBW give designers confidence that FBL has yet to build.
Where FBL suits. Aircraft that face strong EMI or carry fibre near fuel: it flies in production on the Kawasaki P-1 maritime patrol aircraft and on research aircraft.

Evaluation. FBL is better physics for the signal path; FBW wins today on cost, repair and certification experience. As composite airframes (which give less natural screening than aluminium) and higher data rates spread, the balance moves toward fibre.

Closing check. 4.5 + 0.6 + 3.0 = 8.1 dB of loss against 20 dB available leaves 11.9 dB spare; six more connectors (another 4.5 dB) would still close, which shows connectors, not length, are the limit.

bank.q: An aircraft on approach shows a slow pitch oscillation after the autopilot was engaged. Analyse the possible causes in the control loop and the checks you would make.
outline: Identify loop elements: sensor, comparator, control law gain and damping, servo, surface, aircraft dynamics
Sensor fault or lag; lost rate signal
Gain too high for the present q̄; gain schedule fault; glide-slope gain not reduced near the runway
Servo rate limit or backlash; actuator hysteresis
Aircraft changes: speed, configuration, CG
Tests: disengage, fly manually, check signals, gain schedule and servo rigging
answer: The loop to analyse. Pitch channel δe = Kp e − Kr q (e the pitch-attitude error, q the pitch rate), inside an outer loop that holds the glide slope. An oscillation means the loop has too little damping: too much gain, too little rate feedback, or extra lag somewhere.

head: Element
Possible fault
Why it gives a slow pitch oscillation
rows: failed to zero or wrong sign
the K<sub>r</sub> q damping term disappears or reverses
the error arrives late, so corrections arrive late
gains not reduced as q̄ rises
the surface is more effective at higher q̄, so the loop gain grows
gain not reduced as the aircraft nears the runway
the beam narrows, so the same angle error means a smaller height error and the loop over-reacts
a dead zone or lag gives a steady limit cycle
flap change, speed change, aft CG
the airframe’s own pitch damping and stability change

answer: Effect of gain, in numbers. If gains set for q̄ = 6125 Pa (100 m/s) are used at 150 m/s, q̄ is (150 ÷ 100)² = 2.25 times larger, so the elevator’s effect, and the loop gain, are 2.25 times what the designer intended: enough to turn a well-damped loop into an oscillating one.

Effect of losing rate feedback. In the roll example of the autopilot chapter the rate term was 1.6° out of 12°; with it gone the command near the target stays large, the aircraft overshoots, and the proportional term reverses it, giving a sustained oscillation. The pitch channel behaves the same way.

Checks, in order. (1) Disengage the autopilot and fly manually: if the oscillation stops, the fault is in the autopilot loop, not the airframe. (2) Compare the pitch-rate and attitude signals with a second source (standby instruments, the other channel). (3) Check the gain schedule against airspeed and radio altitude in the maintenance data. (4) Check the elevator servo for rate limiting, backlash and correct rigging and clutch setting. (5) Check the weight and balance for an aft CG and the configuration (flap setting) when the oscillation began.

Distinguishing the causes. An oscillation that grows as the aircraft nears the runway points to the glide-slope gain; one that appears only at higher speed points to the gain schedule; a small steady oscillation of fixed size points to servo backlash; one from the moment of engagement points to a sensor or sign fault.

Closing check. (150 ÷ 100)² = 2.25 confirms how strongly an unscheduled gain grows with speed, and every cause in the table acts through the same law δe = Kp e − Kr q, so the checks follow the loop element by element.

glossary.def: A movable aerofoil whose deflection changes the force or moment on the aircraft, such as an aileron, elevator, rudder or flap.
The pitch control surface hinged to the horizontal tailplane, moving the tail lift thus the pitching moment.
A wing trailing-edge surface deflected differentially to produce roll; one goes up while the other goes down.
The yaw control surface on the vertical fin, producing side force and yaw, also used to coordinate turns.
A one-piece horizontal tail that pivots as a whole, used instead of a fixed horizontal stabilizer with a separate elevator.
A small steady deflection or force that holds the aircraft in the desired state without continuous pilot input.
A small hinged tab on a primary surface, set by the pilot so its hinge moment holds the surface deflected with no stick force.
The lever arm on a control surface to which the push-pull rod or cable is attached, setting the mechanical advantage.
Lost motion between linked parts, so a small control input produces no output; it adds free play and can cause flutter.
q = ½ρV², in pascals when ρ is kg/m³ and V is m/s; it sets the aerodynamic force on a surface and hence the feel force.
The ratio of output force to input force of a linkage, the inverse of the ratio of their displacements.
A device that compares a command with a measured position and drives an output until the error is removed.
A valve that meters hydraulic flow in proportion to a small electrical current, giving fast, precise actuator control.
The hydraulic or electric ram that converts a command signal into a force and stroke on a control surface.
A control system in which pilot input is converted to electrical signals and computers command the actuators.
Control-law limiting that prevents the aircraft exceeding angle of attack, load factor, pitch or bank limits whatever the pilot asks.
A degraded FBW mode where pilot inputs pass to the surfaces with simple gearing and no envelope protection.
A system that holds or tracks an attitude, heading, altitude or path by closing the control loop through sensors and servos.
A servo system that drives the throttles automatically to hold a selected speed, thrust or Mach number.
A design where the aircraft is deliberately made slightly unstable and stabilised continuously by the flight control system.
Deflecting surfaces automatically to reduce wing or tail bending loads during gusts and manoeuvres.
Line Replaceable Unit: a box that can be swapped on the flight line without recalibration or deep maintenance.
Full Authority Digital Engine Control: a redundant digital computer that schedules engine fuel and geometry within all limits.
The position of the cockpit thrust lever, the command input to the engine control loop, usually given in degrees.
The ratio of stick travel to surface rotation, in mm per degree or m per radian; it sets both the response and the stick force.
A mass on the elevator linkage that adds stick force in proportion to load factor, so the pilot feels each g.
A pivoted two-armed lever that changes the direction of a rod or cable run, and its motion ratio when the arms differ.
The distance from the centre of gravity aft to the neutral point, as a fraction of the mean aerodynamic chord; positive means statically stable.
A spool speed divided by √θ, the square root of the inlet temperature ratio, so engine behaviour can be compared across temperatures.
